title: Input and maths
bridge: Read input with `std::cin >> variable;`. It reads one word or number at a time and converts it to the variable's type. For a whole line of text use `std::getline(std::cin, line);`. Maths operators are the usual `+ - * / %`, with `/` doing whole-number division for ints.
lesson:
`std::cin` is the keyboard. `>>` pulls a value out of it into a variable:

```
int seconds;
std::cin >> seconds;              // the user types 125
int minutes = seconds / 60;       // 2
int rest = seconds % 60;          // 5
std::cout << minutes << " min " << rest << " s\n";
```

`>>` stops at spaces, so `std::cin >> a >> b;` reads two numbers from `3 4`. For a whole line (a name with a space in it) use `std::getline(std::cin, name);`.

**Rounding up** with whole numbers is a trick you'll use constantly (bags needed, pages needed, trips needed):

```
int bags = (kg + bagSize - 1) / bagSize;   // 100 kg in 30 kg bags -> 4
```

Other maths lives in `<cmath>`: `std::sqrt(x)`, `std::pow(x, 2)`, `std::abs(x)`, `std::round(x)`.

exercises.title: Minutes and seconds
exercises.prompt: Read a number of seconds and print it as minutes and seconds, e.g. 125 prints: 2 min 5 s

exercises.title: Bags needed
exercises.prompt: Write int bagsNeeded(int kg, int bagSize): how many bags to hold all of it (a part-full bag still counts).

tests.hint_if_fail: 100 / 30 is 3, but that leaves 10 kg on the floor. Round up.
